Translator vs interpreter: 8 main differences

November 21, 2023
Translation services | Interpreting | Translators

What is the difference between a translator and an interpreter?

A translator works with written text. An interpreter works with spoken language, in real time. Both move meaning from a source language into a target language, but they use different skills, tools and working conditions.

People often search for “translater” or use the two words as if they were the same job. The correct spelling is “translator”, and getting the distinction right saves you time and budget, whether you are signing a contract in Paris, hosting a supplier visit in Manchester or filing documents with the Home Office.

Below are eight differences that help you decide which service your business needs.

Translator vs interpreter: eight key differences

Written vs spoken language

Translators handle documents, websites, contracts, manuals and marketing copy. They normally translate into their mother tongue and work with dictionaries, glossaries and computer-assisted translation (CAT) tools.

Interpreters handle speech. They listen in one language and speak in another, either after the speaker pauses (consecutive) or at the same time as the speaker (simultaneous). In whispered interpreting, they sit beside one or two listeners and speak quietly.

Need a person to speak for you in a meeting, a hearing or a customer call? You need an interpreter. Need a document, a website or a brochure in another language? You need a translator.

How the work is quoted

Translation is commonly priced by the word or by the page, which makes large document projects easier to plan. Interpreting is commonly priced by the hour or the day, with extra costs for travel, equipment or preparation.

BeTranslated quotes per project for both services. The price depends on the languages, the subject, the volume or duration, and the deadline, so send us the details and you will receive a clear quote.

Working speed

A translator can research terms, check references and revise before delivery. Deadlines still apply, but there is time to refine the text, and a second linguist can proofread it.

An interpreter works at the speed of the conversation. There is no pause button, so preparation before the event matters: send agendas, slides and glossaries in advance.

Language direction

Most professional translators work into their native language, because that is how you achieve natural, idiomatic text.

Interpreters work in both directions, switching between languages as the conversation moves. In a negotiation or a medical appointment, that two-way flow is the whole point.

Location and delivery

Translators have long worked remotely, so you can use specialists wherever they live. Interpreters used to travel to the venue, but remote interpreting by video or phone now covers many meetings, hearings and calls without travel.

For a large conference or a sensitive in-person negotiation, an interpreter on site may still be the better choice. Tell us the format and we will advise.

Tools

Translators use CAT tools, terminology databases and, increasingly, machine translation as a first draft that a human then edits. The right tool depends on the content, and legal, medical and marketing texts need different levels of human review.

Interpreters rely mainly on training, memory and note-taking. Their preparation is a glossary and a briefing, not software.

Precision and flow

A translation can be reviewed, revised and checked until each nuance is right. That makes it the correct choice for contracts, regulatory filings and anything you need to keep as a record.

Interpreting aims for faithful, complete meaning at conversational pace. It suits meetings, interviews and live support, where the exchange has to keep moving.

Qualifications and certification in the UK

Rules differ between the two roles. Home Office visa applications, for example, require a certified translation of any document not in English or Welsh, with the translator’s confirmation that it is an accurate translation, the date, their full name and signature, and their contact details.

For spoken language in public services such as courts, police and the NHS, the National Register of Public Service Interpreters (NRPSI) lists interpreters who meet set qualification and conduct standards. The Diploma in Public Service Interpreting (DPSI), awarded by the Chartered Institute of Linguists, is a Level 6 qualification regulated by Ofqual.

Common business scenarios

A few examples show how the choice works in practice.

  • You are signing a contract with a supplier in France: a translator prepares the contract, and an interpreter supports the signing meeting.
  • You are launching a website in German: a translator adapts the pages, and a specialist checks terminology and tone for your market.
  • You are visiting a factory in Spain: an interpreter, in person or by video, helps you speak with the production team.
  • You are hiring a colleague who needs a UK work or study visa: a certified translator prepares the supporting documents.
  • You are hosting an international webinar: a simultaneous interpreter handles the live session, and a translator can prepare subtitles or a transcript afterwards.

If your project does not fit neatly into one category, describe it to us. Many briefs combine written and spoken work, and a short conversation usually settles the best mix.

Which do you need: a translator or an interpreter?

Match the service to the format of your content. If it is written, such as documents, website pages, marketing material or technical documentation, you need a translator. If it is spoken, such as a meeting, a call, a hearing or an event, you need an interpreter.

Many UK businesses need both. A company expanding into France might translate its contracts and website, then bring in an interpreter for supplier meetings and trade shows. Using one provider for both keeps terminology consistent across the written and spoken side.

BeTranslated supplies specialist translators and interpreters in many language combinations, for clients in London, Manchester, Birmingham and across the UK. Describe your project and request a quote, or call +44 20 3026 9848.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between an interpreter and a translator?

A translator converts written text, while an interpreter converts spoken language in real time. Translators have time to research and revise, and interpreters must deliver the meaning as the conversation happens.

Can one person work as both a translator and an interpreter?

Some linguists do both, but the skills are different. Translation rewards research and careful writing, and interpreting rewards memory, speed and composure, so most professionals specialise in one.

Which do I need for a UK visa or Home Office application?

You need a certified translator for any supporting documents that are not in English or Welsh. If you also attend an interview or appointment in another language, you may need an interpreter as well.

Can I use an interpreter for an online meeting?

Yes. Remote interpreting works by video or phone, and it suits board meetings, supplier calls and customer support. Share your agenda and any technical terms beforehand so the interpreter can prepare.

How are translation and interpreting quoted?

BeTranslated quotes per project. Translation depends on the languages, subject, length and deadline, and interpreting depends on the languages, duration, format and level of preparation required.
